data.approach: Dynamic Programming with Min and Max Tracking
data.key_insight: Because multiplication by a negative number flips the sign of a number, the minimum product can become the maximum product and vice-versa. At each step, we need to maintain both the maximum and minimum product ending at the current position.

steps.title: Initialize variables
steps.detail: Initialize max_product, min_product, and result all to the first element of the array.

steps.title: Iterate through the array
steps.detail: For each subsequent element, if the element is negative, swap the current max_product and min_product.

steps.title: Update products
steps.detail: Update max_product to be the maximum of the current element itself or the current element multiplied by the previous max_product. Similarly, update min_product.

steps.title: Track the global maximum
steps.detail: Update the overall result with the maximum of max_product seen so far.

data.code:
class Solution:
    def maxProduct(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        if not nums:
            return 0
        
        max_so_far = nums[0]
        min_so_far = nums[0]
        result = max_so_far
        
        for i in range(1, len(nums)):
            curr = nums[i]
            temp_max = max_so_far
            
            max_so_far = max(curr, curr * max_so_far, curr * min_so_far)
            min_so_far = min(curr, curr * temp_max, curr * min_so_far)
            
            result = max(result, max_so_far)
            
        return result

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic programming is used when a problem can be broken down into overlapping subproblems, allowing us to store results of previous steps to build up the final solution efficiently.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to track the current max and min products because negative numbers can flip values, building on the results of the previous step.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers usually apply when array elements are sorted or when searching for a window with monotonic properties, which multiplication by negative numbers breaks.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Hash maps are useful for finding complements or frequencies, but subarrays require contiguous elements in a specific sequence.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A purely greedy choice fails here because a locally small or negative product can instantly become the largest product when multiplied by another negative number.

signals.hint: Implies we are dealing with elements that sit next to each other in the array without gaps.
Points to mathematical accumulation where order and sign preservation matter across steps.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach uses three nested loops to check every possible start and end index of every subarray, multiplies all elements within that range, and tracks the highest product found.
data.brute_force_why: There are O(n^2) possible subarrays defined by the start and end indices, and for each subarray, a third loop runs up to O(n) times to compute the product of its elements.
data.bottleneck: Line 7 repeatedly recalculates the product of overlapping subarrays from scratch instead of reusing the product computed in the previous step.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times you visit the same elements across different subarrays.
Notice that the product for subarray nums[i...j] shares almost all its elements with nums[i...j-1].
Ask yourself if you need a third loop to multiply elements, or if you can derive the current product directly from the immediately preceding computation.

data.overview: The Maximum Product Subarray problem finds a contiguous non-empty subarray with the largest product. It tracks both current maximum and minimum products because negative numbers can flip a small product into a large one.
data.intuition: Imagine walking through numbers like juggling positive and negative signs; a very negative number combined with another negative number suddenly becomes a giant positive winner.

pitfalls: Forgetting to track the minimum product and only tracking maximum.
Not handling zeros properly which reset products.
Failing to account for arrays with a single element.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach repeatedly recalculates products for overlapping subarrays using nested loops, leading to cubic time. The optimized approach removes this bottleneck by tracking both the maximum and minimum products ending at the current position, allowing the maximum product to be updated in a single pass using the results of the previous step.

derivation.note: The loop runs for each element from index 1 to n-1.
Assigns the current list element once per iteration.
Stores the previous max_so_far before it gets overwritten.
Computes the maximum of three values in constant time.
Computes the minimum of three values in constant time.
Updates the global result in constant time.

data.time_summary: Lines 11 through 17 execute a constant number of operations inside a single loop of size n. As shown in the measured evidence where n doubles from 4 to 8, the step counts for these lines scale linearly (e.g., line 10 goes from 4 to 8 steps), yielding an overall time complexity of O(n).
data.space_summary: Only a few scalar variables (max_so_far, min_so_far, result, curr, temp_max) are maintained regardless of the input size, resulting in O(1) auxiliary space complexity.
data.takeaway: When a problem involves products or operations where negative numbers can flip extremes, track both the running maximum and minimum states concurrently to maintain valid transitions.
mistakes: Forgetting to track the minimum product, which breaks the logic when a negative number multiplies a negative minimum to produce a large positive maximum.
Failing to store a temporary copy of max_so_far before updating it, causing min_so_far to use the already-mutated max_so_far value.
Returning 0 instead of nums[0] when the array contains a single negative number.
